simulator_description: This simulator models daily patient flow in a hospital with three diseases and two bed types (ICU and standard) by explicitly tracking a roster of individual patients whose length-of-stay counts down over time, discharging them when LOS reaches zero while generating new arrivals each day from disease-specific Poisson rates. Each arrival is probabilistically assigned to ICU versus standard via disease-specific ICU probabilities and receives a sampled geometric LOS with disease- and bed-type-specific means, producing trajectories whose state contains both bed occupancy totals and the full patient list; an optional capacity toggle can reject admissions when beds are full. The structure is sensible because occupancy emerges from micro-level admissions and discharges, the stochastic choices (Poisson arrivals and LOS sampling) are common assumptions in patient-flow models, and the calibration step uses repeated simulations and a neural posterior estimator to tune the 12 key parameters so simulated 7-dimensional summaries (occupancies and alive counts by disease over time) match observed trajectories while enforcing internal consistency between roster and occupancy.

This simulator models daily patient flow in a hospital with two bed types (ICU and Standard) and three disease cohorts, where the state at each day consists of bed occupancies and an explicit roster of individual patients carrying disease label, bed assignment, and remaining length of stay. Each day, existing patients age and are discharged when their LOS reaches zero, then new admissions arrive per disease via a Poisson process, are routed to ICU vs Standard by disease-specific probabilities, and receive LOS draws (preferentially from an empirically learned discrete LOS-at-admission distribution scaled to match disease/bed mean LOS, with a geometric fallback), with optional rejection if capacity limits are enforced. The structure is sensible because it mirrors common census dynamics (arrivals + service times drive occupancy), uses individual agents to ensure occupancy is consistent with the roster, and adds a learned day-varying arrival multiplier to capture nonstationary demand while keeping the core parameterization interpretable and calibratable; calibration then tunes arrival rates, ICU fractions, and LOS means to match observed trajectories.

This simulator models daily patient flow in a hospital with three diseases and two bed types (ICU vs Standard) by maintaining an explicit roster of individual patients whose length of stay counts down each day, discharging them when it reaches zero, and adding new admissions generated from disease-specific Poisson arrival rates. Each arrival is assigned a bed type via a disease-specific ICU probability and a length of stay drawn to match a disease/bed mean, using either a tilted empirical LOS distribution learned from training admissions or a geometric fallback, which is a sensible way to preserve realistic discrete LOS hazards while still allowing parameter control. Occupancy is derived consistently from the roster, optional capacity enforcement can reject admissions, and arrivals include both a smooth time-varying seasonal scaling (estimated from the observed training trajectory to avoid leakage) and deterministic per-trajectory random effects to reflect between-trajectory heterogeneity. A neural posterior estimation calibrator then fits the 12 parameters (arrival rates, ICU probabilities, LOS means) by simulating trajectories and learning a Gaussian posterior mapping from trajectory summaries to parameters, selecting parameters that best reproduce observed occupancy/alive-count dynamics.

This simulator models daily patient flow in a hospital with two bed types (ICU and Standard) and three diseases by evolving an explicit patient roster over time: each day existing patients decrement remaining length-of-stay (LOS) and discharge when it reaches zero, while new disease-specific admissions arrive via Poisson processes, are assigned to ICU vs Standard by disease-specific probabilities, and receive LOS draws whose mean is controlled by parameters but, when possible, is sampled from empirically observed LOS support (tilted to match the target mean) to stay realistic. Bed occupancy is computed directly from the roster to ensure internal consistency, and an optional capacity toggle can reject/divert arrivals when beds are full. A disease-specific time-varying arrival scaling learned from the first training trajectory provides reasonable seasonality without introducing hidden trajectory-id effects, so the structure matches how hospital census emerges from stochastic arrivals and stays while keeping assumptions identifiable and aligned between calibration and evaluation.

The simulator models daily hospital bed occupancy and an explicit roster of in-hospital patients across three diseases by evolving an initial patient list forward in time with stochastic admissions and discharges. Each day, existing patients’ remaining length-of-stay is decremented and those who complete LOS are removed, while new arrivals for each disease are drawn from a time-varying, overdispersed (Gamma–Poisson/negative-binomial) arrival process scaled deterministically by the initial state to reflect cross-trajectory demand differences; each admitted patient is assigned ICU vs Standard via disease-specific probabilities and an LOS drawn from empirically learned discrete distributions (tilted to match target means) or a geometric fallback. Occupancy is computed directly from the roster (with an optional capacity-rejection rule), which makes the state internally consistent and aligns with hospital flow assumptions where arrivals drive census and LOS governs departures, while training-data ingestion of LOS and seasonal arrival profiles grounds the stochastic dynamics in observed patterns.
